claim: Precise heading estimate requires integration of visual optic flow and vestibular inertial motion originating from distinct spatial coordinates (eye- and head-centered, respectively).
source: Precise heading estimate requires integration of visual optic flow and vestibular inertial motion originating from distinct spatial coordinates (eye- and head-centered, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a premise for the study, drawing on established scientific understanding of sensory coordinate systems.

claim: In both FEFsem and MSTd, vestibular signals are head-centered.
source: In both areas, vestibular signals are head-centered, whereas visual signals are mainly eye-centered.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing mean vestibular DI values close to 0 in both areas (FEFsem: 0.14 ± 0.05; MSTd: 0.17 ± 0.08), as shown in Figure 2B,C and described in the Results section.

claim: Visual signals in FEFsem and MSTd are mainly eye-centered.
source: In both areas, vestibular signals are head-centered, whereas visual signals are mainly eye-centered.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mean visual DI values close to 1 (FEFsem: 0.74 ± 0.05; MSTd: 0.95 ± 0.05), as shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Visual signals in FEFsem are more shifted towards the head coordinate compared to MSTd.
source: However, visual signals in FEFsem are more shifted towards the head coordinate compared to MSTd.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of mean visual DI values between areas (FEFsem: 0.74 vs MSTd: 0.95, p=0.005), indicating FEFsem visual signals are less eye-centered than MSTd.

claim: The spatial coordinate findings are largely independent of smooth pursuit eye movement.
source: These results are robust being largely independent on: (1) smooth pursuit eye movement, (2) motion parallax cue, and (3) behavioral context for active heading estimation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that DI values under pursuit are not significantly correlated with DI values under eccentric fixation (FEFsem: p=0.10; MSTd: p=0.82), as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The spatial coordinate findings are largely independent of motion parallax cue.
source: These results are robust being largely independent on: (1) smooth pursuit eye movement, (2) motion parallax cue, and (3) behavioral context for active heading estimation
evidence: This is supported by data showing high correlation between DI values with and without motion parallax (R = 0.70, p=1.5E-7) and no significant difference in means (FEFsem: p=0.37; MSTd: p=0.29), as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The spatial coordinate findings are largely independent of behavioral context for active heading estimation.
source: These results are robust being largely independent on: (1) smooth pursuit eye movement, (2) motion parallax cue, and (3) behavioral context for active heading estimation
evidence: This is supported by data showing high correlation between DI values in passive viewing and active estimation conditions (FEFsem: R = 0.81, p=2.3E-9; MSTd: R = 0.77, p=7.3E-8) with no significant difference in means (FEFsem: p=0.59; MSTd: p=0.55), as shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Visual and vestibular heading signals may be represented in distinct spatial coordinates in sensory cortices.
source: indicating that the visual and vestibular heading signals may be represented in distinct spatial coordinate in sensory cortices.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings showing separated reference frames in both FEFsem and MSTd, with significant differences between visual and vestibular DI values (FEFsem: p=2.2E-7; MSTd: implied by separate distributions).

claim: Human and nonhuman primates can improve heading perception by combining optic flow and vestibular cues in a statistically optimal or near optimal way.
source: Numerous psychophysical studies have shown that human and nonhuman primates can improve heading perception by combining optic flow and vestibular cues in a statistically optimal or near optimal way (Telford et al., 1995; Ohmi, 1996; Harris et al., 2000; Bertin and Berthoz, 2004; Gu et al., 2008; Butler et al., 2010, 2011; Fetsch et al., 2011; Butler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous psychophysical studies.

claim: Visual signals arise from the retina and are represented in an eye-centered coordinate.
source: visual signals arise from the retina and are represented in an eye-centered coordinate
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of visual processing in the nervous system.

claim: Vestibular signals arise from the peripheral organs in the inner ears that are represented in a head-centered coordinate.
source: whereas vestibular signals arise from the peripheral organs in the inner ears that are represented in a head-centered coordinate.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of vestibular processing in the nervous system.

claim: Vision information about heading is often confounded by changes of the eye ball in orbits when subjects vary gaze eccentrically or pursue moving objects.
source: In this case, the vision information about heading is often confounded by changes of the eye ball in orbits, for example, when subjects vary gaze eccentrically or pursue moving objects (Royden et al., 1992; Royden, 1994; Royden et al., 1994; Warren and Saunders, 1995; Banks et al., 1996; Royden and Hildreth, 1996; Crowell et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on eye movements and heading perception.

claim: An intuitive solution to effectively combine visual and vestibular heading cues is to transform them into a common reference frame.
source: An intuitive solution to effectively combine visual and vestibular heading cues is to transform them into a common reference frame (Stein et al., 1993; Cohen and Andersen, 2002).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposition supported by citations to previous computational and theoretical work.

claim: The hypothesis that visual and vestibular signals are transformed into a common reference frame has not been supported by neurophysiological findings in mid-stage sensory areas including VIP and MSTd.
source: Nevertheless, so far this hypothesis has not been supported by neurophysiological findings in mid-stage sensory areas including the ventral intraparietal area (VIP) and the dorsal portion of the medial superior temporal area (MSTd) (Avillac et al., 2005; Fetsch et al., 2007; Takahashi et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neurophysiological studies in VIP and MSTd.

claim: In VIP and MSTd, the spatial reference frame remains largely separated such that the visual optic flow signals are mainly eye-centered and the vestibular signals are mainly head/body centered.
source: Specifically, the spatial reference frame remains largely separated in these areas such that the visual optic flow signals are mainly eye-centered and the vestibular signals are mainly head/body centered.
evidence: This claim is based on previous neurophysiological findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: FEFsem receives heavy inputs from MSTd and is closer to the motor side.
source: Therefore, in the current study we targets on an area at a later stage in the dorsal visual pathway: the smooth pursuit area of the frontal eye field, that is FEFsem, which receives heavy inputs from MSTd and is closer to the motor side (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Fukushima, 2003; Lynch and Tian, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical and connectivity studies.

claim: FEFsem contains robust visual and vestibular signals that may contribute to heading estimation.
source: Similar to MSTd, this area also contains robust visual and vestibular signals that may contribute to heading estimation (Gu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on FEFsem.

claim: Some researchers have measured tuning curves in a limited heading range that could have confounded tuning shift versus gain change.
source: First, some researchers have measured tuning curves in a limited heading range that could have confounded tuning shift versus gain change (Bradley et al., 1996; Bremmer et al., 1997a; Bremmer et al., 1997b; Page and Duffy, 1999; Shenoy et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a methodological critique supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Smooth eye movement compensation experiments are not necessarily linked with spatial reference frame which should have been measured under different static eye positions.
source: Second, people have conducted smooth eye movement compensation experiments (Bradley et al., 1996; Zhang et al., 2004) that are not necessarily linked with spatial reference frame which should have been measured under different static eye positions (Fetsch et al., 2007; Takahashi et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2013; Sunkara et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological critique supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Available depth cues such as motion parallax are not consistent across previous studies.
source: Third, available depth cues such as motion parallax are not consistent across the above studies.
evidence: This is an observation about methodological inconsistencies in the literature.

claim: Previous studies have measured visual tuning curves under passive viewing tasks where visual signals are not obliged to be transformed towards a head-centered reference frame for heading judgments.
source: Last but not least, people have measured visual tuning curves under passive viewing tasks (Fetsch et al., 2007; Takahashi et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2013; Sunkara et al., 2015). In such a behavioral context, the visual signals are not obliged to be transformed towards a head-centered reference frame for heading judgments.
evidence: This is a methodological critique supported by citations and logical inference about task demands.

claim: 171 neurons in FEFsem were significantly tuned to visual optic flow.
source: This part of experiment included 171 neurons significantly tuned to visual optic flow and 71 neurons significantly tuned to inertial motion in FEFsem.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data collection.

claim: 71 neurons in FEFsem were significantly tuned to inertial motion.
source: This part of experiment included 171 neurons significantly tuned to visual optic flow and 71 neurons significantly tuned to inertial motion in FEFsem.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data collection.

source: In MSTd, 99 and 54 neurons that were significantly tuned to optic flow and inertial motion, respectively, were included in the final dataset
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data collection.

source: A DI value of 1 means a complete shift of the tuning curve relative to the change in eye position (20°) and thus indicates an eye-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is a definition of the displacement index metric used in the analysis.

claim: Smooth pursuit is frequently accompanied during spatial navigation and could potentially distort perceived flow field.
source: In addition to the static eye fixations varied at different eccentricities, other type of eye behavior, such as smooth pursuit is also frequently accompanied during spatial navigation which could potentially distort perceived flow field (Warren and Hannon, 1988, 1990; Royden et al., 1992; Banks et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on pursuit and heading perception.

claim: Some studies have used smooth pursuit paradigm to infer cortical neurons' spatial coordinate.
source: In fact, some studies have used smooth pursuit paradigm to infer cortical neurons' spatial coordinate (Bradley et al., 1996; Page and Duffy, 1999; Shenoy et al., 1999, 2002; Ilg et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about previous methodological approaches supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies argued that pursuit compensations are not necessarily linked to spatial reference frames as measured under varied static eye positions.
source: However, recent studies argued that the more or less pursuit compensations as observed in these studies is not necessarily linked to spatial reference frames as measured under varied static eye positions during stimulus presentation (Sunkara et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about recent findings supported by a citation.

claim: For neurons with lateral heading preference (0°/180°), tuning peak and trough remain unchanged during pursuit, but responses at the two sides of the tuning peak are shifted in opposite directions.
source: Specifically, for neurons with lateral heading preference (0°/180°, top left panel in Figure 4B), tuning peak and trough remain unchanged. Instead, responses at the two sides of the tuning peak are shifted in opposite directions, causing the overall bandwidth increases or decreases for leftward or rightward pursuit, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of expected tuning curve changes during pursuit for neurons with specific heading preferences, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: For neurons with forward/backward heading preference (90°/270°), the tuning peak and trough are shifted in opposite directions during pursuit, causing a change of the tuning width.
source: For neurons with forward/backward heading preference (90°/270°, top right panel in Figure 4B), the tuning peak and trough are shifted in opposite directions, also causing a change of the tuning width.
evidence: This is a description of expected tuning curve changes during pursuit for neurons with specific heading preferences, illustrated in Figure 4B.

source: In this case, a DI value of 1 means complete tuning shift and implies that the neuron responds to resultant optic flow due to eye rotations.
evidence: This is a definition of the DI metric in the context of the pursuit protocol.

claim: Even complete eye rotation compensation for simulated heading observed in cortical neurons does not necessarily imply a head-centered spatial reference frame.
source: Thus, even complete eye rotation compensation for simulated heading observed in cortical neurons (e.g. FEFsem and MSTd) does not necessarily imply a head-centered spatial reference frame.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of correlation between pursuit compensation and spatial reference frame measures.

claim: Depth cue such as motion parallax plays an important role in deciphering self-motion based on the depth structure of a visual scene.
source: Depth cue such as motion parallax plays an important role in deciphering self-motion based on the depth structure of a visual scene (Gibson, 1950; von Helmholtz, 1963)

We discover that there is no significant relationship between the two metrics computed from the two experimental conditions.
